name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,374

clue.text: What contains books, fish and net? (9)

blocks.note: a school is a shoal of fish swimming together
to net a catch is to bag it

annotation.surface: A riddle about some odd container holding reading matter, a fish and a net.
annotation.walkthrough: "Fish" and "net" look like a fisherman's haul, but the fish is a whole shoal and the net is a verb meaning to capture.
annotation.definitionFit: A schoolbag is the satchel a pupil carries textbooks in, so 'what contains books' describes it by its job.

clue.text: Fire rifle (4)

blocks.note: to fire an employee is to dismiss them from the job
to rifle a place is to ransack or plunder it

annotation.surface: Two words from the firing range: shoot the gun.
annotation.walkthrough: Both words look like guns and shooting, but each is a verb with a different sense: dismissing a worker, and looting a town.
annotation.definitionFit: Sack means both to dismiss someone from a job, as fire does, and to pillage, as rifle does when you rifle through a house.

clue.text: Most valuable baseball hit in career (4,3)

blocks.note: someone who is in is at home
to career is to rush along at speed, to run

annotation.surface: A sports stat: the best hit of a baseball player's career.
annotation.walkthrough: "In career" reads like a phrase about a player's lifetime, but "in" and "career" each supply a word, and career is the verb for hurtling along.
annotation.definitionFit: A home run scores the batter and every runner on base in one swing, so it is the most valuable hit in baseball.

clue.text: Member of parliament’s constituents from Cowley (3)

indicators.note: constituents are the parts a thing is made of, so the answer is made of letters taken from the next word

blocks.note: the answer sits in the middle of the place name, between its C and its EY

annotation.surface: A British MP and the voters of the Cowley area of Oxford.
annotation.walkthrough: Constituents and a member of parliament make this look like politics; a parliament is also the collective noun for a group of owls.
annotation.definitionFit: A group of owls is called a parliament, so any single owl is a member of one.

clue.text: Lie about US agent’s hit (6)

indicators.note: 'about' as in turned about, facing the other way, so the word it governs is read backwards

blocks.note: a lie is a FIB, written backwards
a Fed is an FBI agent in American slang; the 's is 'is', joining wordplay to definition

annotation.surface: A news line about a lie told concerning an American agent's hit job.
annotation.walkthrough: "Hit" reads as a contract killing, but it is the definition, a plain punch.
annotation.definitionFit: To biff someone is informal British and Canadian English for hitting them, so biffed is a plain synonym for hit.

clue.text: Fairness seems to follow virtue (4,5)

indicators.note: to follow is to come after, so the word before it is placed after the word that comes next

blocks.note: virtue is goodness, the good
he seems tired = he looks tired

annotation.surface: A moral maxim: justice appears to go hand in hand with virtue.
annotation.walkthrough: "Fairness" sounds like justice beside "virtue", but here it is fair in the sense of beautiful.
annotation.definitionFit: Fair has an old sense of beautiful, as in 'fair maiden', so fairness is attractiveness, good looks.

clue.text: Mock company director’s first letter (3)

indicators.note: says outright to take only the opening letter of the word before it

blocks.note: Co. is the standard abbreviation for company
the first letter of director

annotation.surface: Someone ridicules the opening letter written by a firm's director.
annotation.walkthrough: "Mock" looks like a verb, to ridicule, but the answer is the adjective, fake.
annotation.definitionFit: Cod is British informal for mock or sham, as in a cod accent or cod philosophy.

clue.text: He thinks the worst of people in fancy niches (5)

definitions.text: He thinks the worst of people

indicators.note: the answer is literally in the words that follow, sitting inside them

blocks.note: the answer straddles the gap, taking the last two letters of fancy and the first three of niches

annotation.surface: A misanthrope who suspects anyone with an expensive little alcove.
annotation.walkthrough: "Fancy" looks like an anagram signal for "niches", but nothing is rearranged; the answer straddles the gap between the two words.
annotation.definitionFit: A cynic distrusts others' motives and assumes the worst of them, so the definition is a plain description of the type.

clue.text: Smart doctor starts to examine serious case of scurvy (6)

indicators.note: the starts of words are their first letters
a case is the outside that holds something, so the case of a word is its outer letters

blocks.note: Dr is the standard abbreviation for doctor
the first letters of examine and serious
the first and last letters of scurvy

annotation.surface: A clever doctor begins examining a severe case of scurvy.
annotation.walkthrough: "Smart" suggests a clever doctor, but it is the definition in its sense of well dressed, and "case" is a wrapper, not a patient.
annotation.definitionFit: Smart clothes are dressy ones, both meaning stylish and formal in appearance.

clue.text: Animal arrived then left (5)

blocks.note: past tense of come
L is the standard abbreviation for left

annotation.surface: An animal that turned up and then went away again.
annotation.walkthrough: "Arrived then left" sounds like a brief visit, but "left" is the direction, reduced to its letter.
annotation.definitionFit: A camel is an animal; the definition is the broad class it belongs to.

clue.text: Petulant move of uncle getting upset (7)

indicators.note: to upset is to knock over, so the letters before it are tipped out of order

blocks.note: the anagram fodder

annotation.surface: A sulky gesture from an uncle who has become upset.
annotation.walkthrough: "Of" looks like a joining word, but its two letters are part of the mix.
annotation.definitionFit: To flounce is to storm off with exaggerated, impatient movements, so a flounce is exactly a petulant move.

clue.text: Bricks stop piercing winds (6,6)

indicators.note: something piercing another thing goes inside it, so the first word is put inside the second

blocks.note: breezes are light winds
to stop something is to block it

annotation.surface: A wall of bricks that keeps out cutting, bitter winds.
annotation.walkthrough: "Piercing winds" reads as a cold gale, but piercing is the instruction to push one word inside the other.
annotation.definitionFit: Breeze blocks are the lightweight building blocks made from cinder ash, used like large bricks; Canadians call them cinder blocks.

clue.text: Suppose social worker, for example, is with child (9)

blocks.note: I expect so = I suppose so
a worker ant is an example of a social insect

annotation.surface: A social worker is pregnant, supposedly.
annotation.walkthrough: "Social worker" is a job in the surface; in the wordplay it is a worker ant, one of the social insects, and "for example" flags it as one instance.
annotation.definitionFit: An expectant mother is pregnant, and 'with child' is the old phrase for pregnant.

clue.text: Cut nails back (4)

indicators.note: going back means travelling in the opposite direction, so the word is read from its end

blocks.note: nails are PINS, read backwards

annotation.surface: An instruction at the manicurist's: trim the fingernails short.
annotation.walkthrough: "Nails" belongs to fingers in the surface; the wordplay wants the carpenter's kind, pins.
annotation.definitionFit: To snip is to cut with small quick strokes of scissors.

clue.text: I goofed up over operations (4)

definitions.note: The definition is a whole sentence of apology, and oops is the interjection that says it.

blocks.note: O is the cricket scorer's abbreviation for an over
ops is the short form of operations, as in military ops

annotation.surface: Someone admits a blunder in how operations were run.
annotation.walkthrough: "Up over" looks like a direction for placing letters, but "up" belongs to the definition, and over is the cricket abbreviation.
annotation.definitionFit: Oops is what you say at the moment you realise you have made a mistake, so it stands for 'I goofed up'.

clue.text: Professional sporting event in March? (7)

blocks.note: a pro is a professional
a Test is an international cricket or rugby match

annotation.surface: A professional sports fixture held in the month of March.
annotation.walkthrough: The capital M makes March the month, but it is a demonstration march, and the question mark says the definition is by example.
annotation.definitionFit: A march through the streets is one form a protest takes, so the answer is defined by one example.

clue.text: Sound of person expelling air from lungs and chest (6)

indicators.note: asks for how a word sounds, not how it is spelt

blocks.note: someone who coughs forces air from the lungs, a cougher

annotation.surface: A doctor listening to a patient's lungs and chest as they breathe out.
annotation.walkthrough: "Lungs and chest" look like one body, but "chest" is split off as the definition, a strongbox.
annotation.definitionFit: A coffer is a strongbox or chest for holding money and valuables.

clue.text: Small burger in new deli’s range to begin with (6)

indicators.note: a new version of something is made over, so the letters are rearranged
what comes to begin with is at the start, so only the first letter is taken

blocks.note: DELIS, rearranged
the first letter of range

annotation.surface: A mini burger that a new delicatessen offers as a starter.
annotation.walkthrough: "Deli’s" counts its S as a letter, since the possessive is written like a plural.
annotation.definitionFit: A slider is North American slang for a small burger, served in bites on a little bun.

clue.text: Article less about instructive experience (6,6)

blocks.note: an article is a thing, an object
the word taken as it stands
a talk on something is about it

annotation.surface: An editor asks for a shorter piece about something educational.
annotation.walkthrough: "Article" makes you think of a newspaper piece or a grammatical 'the'; here it is simply a thing.
annotation.definitionFit: An object lesson is a practical example that teaches something vividly, an instructive experience.

clue.text: Joy failing to finish drink in large bowl (5)

indicators.note: a word that fails to finish never reaches its last letter, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: JOY with its last letter removed
the Y that is dropped
rum is a spirit, a drink

annotation.surface: A cheerful person who never finishes her drink out of a huge bowl.
annotation.walkthrough: "Joy" reads as a woman's name or delight; either way only its first two letters are used.
annotation.definitionFit: A jorum is an old word for a large drinking bowl, and by extension the drink it holds.

clue.text: Boom box (4)

blocks.note: a boom is the pole along the foot of a sail, one of a ship's poles
to box for practice, with a partner, uses a four-letter verb

annotation.surface: A loudspeaker, the boom box of the 1980s.
annotation.walkthrough: "Boom box" is one object, a portable stereo; split it into a sailing pole and a verb for fighting.
annotation.definitionFit: A spar is any pole on a ship, a boom among them, and sparring is boxing practice with a partner.

clue.text: Send on attacker (7)

blocks.note: to send on mail is to pass it along to a new address
an attacker in hockey, soccer or rugby plays up front

annotation.surface: A coach sending an attacking player onto the field.
annotation.walkthrough: "Send on" sounds like a substitution in sport, but it means passing a letter along.
annotation.definitionFit: Forward is the verb for sending post or email on, and the noun for a player who plays up front to attack.

clue.text: Give birth with assistance (5)

blocks.note: W is short for with, as in w/
help is assistance

annotation.surface: A mother delivering her baby with a midwife's help.
annotation.walkthrough: "With" looks like a joining word but shrinks to its single letter.
annotation.definitionFit: To whelp is to give birth, used of dogs and some other animals.

clue.text: You and I filled with love and grief (3)

indicators.note: something filled with another thing holds it inside, so the second word goes into the first

blocks.note: you and I together are we
love is zero in tennis scoring, the letter O

annotation.surface: A couple overwhelmed by both love and sorrow.
annotation.walkthrough: "Love and grief" pairs two emotions, but love is the tennis nil and grief stands apart as the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Woe is deep sorrow, a plain synonym for grief.

clue.text: Crash into back of car in the morning (3)

indicators.note: the back of a word is its end, so only its last letter is taken

blocks.note: the last letter of car
a.m. marks the morning hours

annotation.surface: A rear-end collision during the morning commute.
annotation.walkthrough: "Back of car" sounds like where a crash hits; it is where the letter is taken from.
annotation.definitionFit: To ram something is to crash into it deliberately and hard.

clue.text: Men in high places persecuting individual (9)

indicators.note: one thing in another is inside it, so the first word goes between the letters of the second

blocks.note: a tor is a rocky hilltop, and the plural gives two of them
the word taken as it stands

annotation.surface: Powerful men in top positions picking on one person.
annotation.walkthrough: "Men in high places" is the idiom for the powerful; read literally, the men stand between two tors, the rocky hills of Dartmoor and the West Country.
annotation.definitionFit: A tormentor is someone who persecutes or torments another, so the definition describes the person by what they do.
